content_voiceover: This is the structure of fibrinogen, the substrate that thrombin ultimately acts on. Fibrinogen is a dimer, and each half is made of three polypeptide chains, an A alpha chain, a B beta chain, and a gamma chain, held together by disulfide bonds, so you really have six chains total arranged symmetrically. Structurally the molecule is organized into five domains along its length, a D domain at each end, a coiled coil segment connecting each D domain to the center, and a central E domain where the two halves of the molecule join. The amino termini of the alpha and beta chains cluster in that central E domain, and each one carries a small peptide capped off the end, fibrinopeptide A on the alpha chain and fibrinopeptide B on the beta chain. These fibrinopeptides are essentially caps that mask the polymerization sites and keep fibrinogen soluble in plasma. Until they're removed, fibrinogen cannot polymerize into fibrin, which is exactly what happens next when thrombin gets involved.
keypoints: Fibrinogen is a dimer of three chains each, A alpha, B beta, and gamma
Structure has two D domains, two coiled coils, and a central E domain
Fibrinopeptide A caps the alpha chain, fibrinopeptide B caps the beta chain
Fibrinopeptides mask polymerization sites, keeping fibrinogen soluble
Removal of fibrinopeptides is the trigger for fibrin polymerization
keypoint_voiceover: Fibrinogen is a symmetric dimer built from A alpha, B beta, and gamma chains, organized into D domains, coiled coils, and a central E domain. Fibrinopeptides A and B cap the amino termini in that E domain and keep the molecule soluble until they're cleaved off.
